rationale: Across discovery and expansion cohorts, developmental delay and speech/language impairment represent hallmark features of Fliedner-Zweier syndrome (SCAF4-related disorder). In the initial cohort (Fliedner et al., 2020), speech development was noted to be more severely affected than motor milestones or global cognition. Further delineation in an expanded cohort of 50 individuals (Tran Mau et al., 2025) confirmed that speech impairment and mild developmental delay are predominant findings, while formal cognitive outcomes demonstrate wide expressivity ranging from normal IQ and borderline cognitive function to severe intellectual disability, demonstrating that speech impairment is indeed more consistently penetrant than formal intellectual disability.

evidence.text: In the initial cohort identifying nine individuals with SCAF4 variants, developmental delay and mild intellectual disability were noted, with speech acquisition noted to be more severely delayed than other neurodevelopmental domains.

new_directions.question_text: What specific subdomains of speech and language (e.g., expressive versus receptive language, speech apraxia, or articulation) are predominantly impaired in SCAF4-related disorder?
new_directions.rationale: Standardizing psychometric and logopedic evaluations across existing cohorts will clarify whether the speech phenotype is distinct from general developmental delay and whether it can serve as a diagnostic discriminator.

new_directions.question_text: Do specific missense variants in the CTD-interacting domain lead to milder neurocognitive phenotypes compared to truncating variants?
new_directions.rationale: Structural modeling suggests differential destabilization by missense variants; comparing formal IQ and language milestones across variant classes will establish genotype-phenotype correlations.
